Power, Machiavelli argues, is kept by being feared rather than loved when both cannot be had, promises are tools to be judged by outcomes, and fortune favors the bold who act. He describes power as it is practiced, not as moralists said it should be. Five centuries of argument over his name began with these chapters.
tob-3002:
Augustine of Hippo's Confessions, in E. B. Pusey's translation, trace his path from restless North African youth to Christian bishop. A stolen pear, a brilliant career in rhetoric, years with the Manichaeans, and a mother's prayers fill the early books. Conversion comes in a Milan garden, under a child's voice chanting take up and read.

Late have I loved thee, O Beauty ever ancient, ever new, runs his famous cry. The final books turn from story to memory, time, and Genesis, in thirteen books that effectively invented spiritual autobiography in Western literature. Pusey, an Oxford churchman, keeps the passion of the Latin in dignified English. The examined life starts here for many readers.
tob-0202:
The Kybalion opens with a key line: as above, so below. The 1908 Hermetic classic teaches mental transmutation. That is, the art of changing one's inner state to change one's world. Seven rules, said to come down from Hermes of old Egypt, carry the whole teaching. The Three Initiates wrote for doers, not for scholars.

Mind, matching, rhythm, the pull of opposites, cause and effect: each rule is stated, then glossed, then put to use. The book is the New Thought world's most lasting handbook, still in print and still quoted. Its plain style is the point. Seven rules, meant to be used each day.
tob-0102:
Abraham of Worms left an account of learning sacred magic from Abramelin, an Egyptian mage he met in his travels. Book one of the Sacred Magic of Abramelin tells that story. Abraham writes for his son, explaining why the true magic differs from the frauds and dark rites around him.

The prize is the Knowledge and Conversation of the Holy Guardian Angel, won through many months of prayer and a purified life. Book one sets out the journey, the teacher, and the rules of conduct. Few magical books demand so much of the reader. Later magicians, Crowley among them, treated the work as a summit.
tob-4102:
Kenneth James Saunders, scholar and missionary, translated the Dhammapada from the Pali under the title The Buddha's Way of Virtue. His 1919 edition carries introduction and notes for the general reader. The 423 verses of the original form the best-known summary of the Buddha's teaching.

Mind goes before all things, the opening verse declares; a trained mind brings happiness like a shadow that never leaves. Saunders renders the Pali with respect and a light touch. His notes explain terms from Buddhist practice for Western ears. Verified from the 1919 edition, the little book serves as a gentle, scholarly first step into Buddhist ethics.
tob-9102:
Melody rules the Sama Veda, the Veda of chants, in Griffith's translation verified from the 1919 scan. Its verses are mostly Rigvedic lines reset for singing at the soma sacrifice. Priests stretched and ornamented the words until the chant became an art of its own.

As a book of words, the Sama Veda is the shortest of the four Vedas. As a book of music, it is the root from which Indian classical singing claims descent. Griffith prints the verses in the order singers used them. Readers meet the Veda that exists to be heard, the liturgy behind the hymns found elsewhere.
tob-10402:
Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria, spent much of his life fighting the teaching of Arius, who said Christ was a created being, not fully God. His discourses Against the Arians form his fullest defense of the Nicene faith. Enemies exiled him five times, yet he kept writing.

He argues from scripture that the Word is true God, of one being with the Father, and that only a divine savior can save mankind. The discourses mix close Bible reading with sharp attacks on his foes. They helped secure the doctrine of the Trinity in the church and remain a base text of early Christian theology.
tob-14502:
Jalaluddin Rumi, the thirteenth-century Sufi master of Konya, composed the Masnavi, a vast poem in six books in Persian. He dictated it to a disciple over many years. Persian speakers have called it the Quran in Persian for its depth.

Story follows story: kings, fools, lovers, and animals act out lessons on the soul's longing for God. The opening song of the reed flute, cut from its reed bed, sets the theme of separation and return. Rumi breaks off tales to comment, joke, and pray. It is the most read poem in the Muslim world and a summit of Sufi teaching.
govdocs-archive_org-ProjectSCANATECIARDP:
Project SCANATE was an early CIA effort to test remote viewing, the claimed ability to describe distant places using only the mind. The declassified file preserves the agency's own paperwork on that research, approved for public release in 2003.

Inside are the records of a program that treated psychic perception as a possible tool for gathering intelligence during the Cold War. The papers show officials taking the idea seriously enough to fund and file formal studies of it. For readers, the file is direct evidence of how far intelligence agencies were willing to go in the 1970s.

Filed under the CIA's own name, a second copy of the Project SCANATE document holds the agency's early study of remote viewing. The research centered on Ingo Swann at SRI, who reported that he could view far-off locations without leaving the room.

The papers record how the agency set up and judged those tests, and they were approved for release in 2003. Keeping this duplicate matters because releases can differ in small ways, and researchers compare copies line by line. Together with its twin file, it documents the first step in the government's long remote-viewing program.
govdocs-archive_org-ks_-_cia_vault_8_201:
On November 9, 2017, WikiLeaks published Vault 8, source code and technical analysis from the CIA's Hive project. The release belonged to the long Vault 7 series of CIA hacking documents that WikiLeaks issued through 2017. It was the eighth installment in that series.

Hive was the agency's system for controlling implanted malware on target computers while hiding the CIA's hand in the operation. Vault 8 went past description to the code itself, together with analysis meant for technically minded readers. It is kept complete for researchers of cyber history and of the leak era, when secret tools became public documents.
govdocs-archive_org-ting_environment_201: WikiLeaks released the CIA's Vault 8 material on HIVE, a piece of agency hacking infrastructure. The HIVE operating environment papers describe the environment in which that system ran. Vault releases show the tools behind public headlines about state hacking. Technical readers can study how the environment was organized in 2012. The release is held as a United States government document taken from the archive's holdings.
hale-modest-enquiry-witchcraft-1702:
John Hale was pastor at Beverly, near Salem, and at first he backed the witch trials of 1692. A Modest Enquiry into the Nature of Witchcraft, printed at Boston in 1702, is his second look at that hard year. He wrote it after doubt had time to grow.

Hale asks what witchcraft is, how a guilty person can be proved, and how the innocent can be kept safe. He casts doubt on spectral proof, claims based on visions only the accusers could see. Scripture and hard experience guide his argument on both sides. The book is the first clear critique of Salem from a man inside it.
lybeaus-desconus-weston-1902:
Jessie Weston turned the English Fair Unknown romance into plain modern prose in 1902. Sir Libeaus Desconus renders the medieval poem of the knight who did not know his own name. Weston's clear prose was made for readers new to such tales.

Libeaus comes to Arthur's court a raw youth, is mocked for his looks, and rides out to prove himself. Fights, rescues, and a lady freed from sorcery mark his road to honor. The tale is the English twin of the French Bel Inconnu. Weston's version keeps the story whole while dropping the hard old verse.
joan-arc-trial-murray-1902:
Douglas Murray's 1902 English rendering brings both of Joan of Arc's trials to readers in one book. The Trial of Jeanne d'Arc pairs the condemnation of 1431 with the rehabilitation of the 1450s. English readers long met the records first in Murray's pages.

The first trial shows Joan questioned at Rouen and sent to the fire as a heretic. The second shows a new court hearing the same ground and clearing her name in full. Set side by side, the two records frame one of the great reversals in legal history. The book is the classic English door into the Joan file.
dioscorides-materia-medica-berendes-1902:
Pedanius Dioscorides, a Greek doctor of the first century, wrote the founding book of drug lore. De Materia Medica, in Julius Berendes's German rendering of 1902, gives his five books whole. Doctors lived by this text for more than fifteen hundred years.

Dioscorides lists hundreds of plants, stones, and animal parts, with the use and dose of each. He tells how to know the true drug from the false and how to store each kind. His plain, tested style set the form of drug books for ages. Berendes's version opened the Greek master to German readers.
bellingshausen-forschungsfahrten-suedlic:
Fabian von Bellingshausen sailed for the far south in 1819 with two Russian ships and orders to push past all prior tracks. His account, in the German edition of 1902, tells that voyage of 1819 to 1821. His ships were the first to sight the mainland of Antarctica.

Six chapters run from Kronstadt out to the ice, along the new-found coast, and home again. Bellingshausen tells of storms, ice fields, new islands, and the hardships of his crews in plain naval prose. The sighting of a new continent gives the book its lasting rank. It is the record of one of the great firsts of exploration.
crowley-equinox-vol-1-no-02:
September 1909 brought the second number of Crowley's great journal, The Equinox. The Equinox, volume one, number two, keeps the twice-yearly pace he set for the work. The journal served as the public record of his order and its teaching.

Fresh rites and teaching papers saw print here first, as they did in each number. Verse, reviews, and tall tales fill out the bulk beside the grave matter. The whole run of the journal is the prime source for the birth of Thelema. Number two shows the young venture in full and confident stride. Its white bulk set the look of all the numbers to come.
jacobs-lady-of-the-barge-1902:
W. W. Jacobs mixed sea tales and dark tales in The Lady of the Barge and Others, his set from 1902. Most tales are brisk and wry. Sailors spin yarns, con men scheme, and small folk meet odd turns of luck in port towns.

One tale towers past the rest. In it, a paw plucked from a mummy grants three wishes, and each wish turns to grief. That tale is now the most famed short fright tale in the tongue. It taught hosts of scribes how dread can grow from one small, plain choice. Jacobs, a clerk turned scribe, had a keen ear for dock side talk. That ear makes both the jokes and the dread feel true to life.
podmore-modern-spiritualism-1902:
Frank Podmore wrote the chief cool past of a faith in Modern Spiritualism, his two tome work of 1902. Podmore was the top doubt voice in the band that made such things its study. He knew the dark room from the in side. Here he tells the faith's tale from the Fox girls to his own day, fraud by fraud.

His tone is fair, dry, and oft wry. He grants some strange scraps, yet finds fraud at the root of most fame. All pasts of the theme since cite his work. It is the faith judged by its best foe.
trunko-watauga-democrat-1925-04-02:
A strange bulk fights the sea in the Watauga Democrat piece of April 2, 1925. The North Carolina paper reprints a tale from Margate, on the coast of South Africa, from the year past. There, guests watched a vast hairy beast fight two whales for hours. It looked like a polar bear grown huge. It then lay dead on the sand, lost ere it could be gauged for science.

Locals named the beast Trunko in lore since then. No proof of it was kept at all. The reprint is the root source of the whole tale. Its loss is the point.
johnston-uganda-protectorate-vol1-1902:
Harry Johnston finds a beast men called a fable in Vol. 1 of The Uganda Protectorate, out in 1902. Johnston ran the new state in the heart of Africa for Britain. His tome maps its lands, folk, beasts, and trade. Midst it stands his tale of the okapi: a shy beast of the deep woods, part horse, part zebra in hue, known to the tribes yet hid from science till his day.

Skins and bones sent home proved the beast was real. That find stunned the age. The tome is both a state book and a beast tale. It is a rich store.
johnston-uganda-protectorate-vol2-1902:
Harry Johnston ends his great survey in Vol. 2 of The Uganda Protectorate, out in 1902. The first tome gave the land's frame and the okapi's debut. Here the tale runs on through the state's tribes, faiths, crops, and wild life in dense, rich parts. The okapi's tale is brought to its close as more skins, bones, and notes reach the schools of the West from the deep woods.

Johnston writes as both chief and sage of life. His draws and plates fill the tome. The pair is the set book on the land for its age. Its scope still stuns.
young-theory-light-colours-1802:
Thomas Young, an English doctor and sage, read this Bakerian Lecture on light and hues across 1801 and 1802. Most men of his day held that light was a stream of tiny parts. Young held that light moves in waves, like sound through air.

His proof rests on the way light bands form when rays cross and mix. He showed the bands fit waves that add and cancel, not parts that fly straight. The wave view made a stuff called the ether seem a need, since waves must wave in something. The talk is still the root text of the wave view.
rhodes-last-will-testament-1902:
Cecil John Rhodes built a vast fortune in South African diamonds and gold, and he died in 1902 leaving a series of wills. Those wills set out how his money should be used after his death. Journalist W. T. Stead edited the wills for print that same year, adding long notes to explain them.

Readers find the actual terms Rhodes left behind, including money for scholarships and for grand plans in Africa. Stead's notes spell out the secret aims Rhodes attached to some gifts, aims later tied to the Round Table movement. Few books show so plainly how one rich man hoped to shape an empire from the grave.
leadbeater-man-visible-invisible-1902:
C. W. Leadbeater said he could see the fine forms that clothe each soul. His Man Visible and Invisible came out in 1902. It claims to show men as they look to trained clairvoyant sight. Bright plates in the book paint auras and thought forms round the head.

Leadbeater sorts men by the hues and forms his sight found in them. Saints glow in calm tints, while base moods cloud the form. The book set the look of the aura for the whole New Age field. Few theosophy books have been copied so much in art and print.
defoe-shortest-way-with-the-dissenters-1:
Daniel Defoe published The Shortest Way with the Dissenters in 1702, a savage ironic pamphlet in prose. The tract urges, in a High Church voice, the persecution and hanging of Protestant Dissenters in England. Taken literally by both sides, it led to his prosecution, pillorying, and ruin in 1703 by law.

Defoe mimics a zealot so well that Anglicans applauded and Dissenters trembled before the hoax broke open. His point was that persecution's logic ends at the gallows, whatever soft words clothe it at first. The state read sedition in the irony, fined him, and stood him in the pillory three days. Crowds drank his health and threw flowers, and he wrote a hymn to the pillory from prison. The affair made Defoe famous and broke him, the making of the later novelist.
strindberg-the-dream-play-1902:
August Strindberg wrote The Dream Play in 1902, here in Edwin Björkman's English translation for Western readers. The daughter of Indra descends to earth in the dream-drama that invented expressionist theatre for the modern stage. Strindberg's preface bids actors imitate the disjointed but seemingly logical shape of a dream in performance throughout.

Indra's daughter, as Agnes, marries, suffers, and watches human life repeat its pains in shifting scenes. An Officer waits for a singer who never comes, and a Lawyer wears mankind's grievances in his face. A castle grows from a dung heap, and a door with a cloverleaf hole guards life's secret. Humanity's refrain, men are to be pitied, tolls through scene changes that melt like thoughts in sleep. Björkman's version seeded the play's immense influence on theatre, film, and the modernist stage.
maupassant-necklace-stories-1902:
Guy de Maupassant's The Necklace and Other Short Stories gathers thirteen of his sharpest tales dress. The title tale, The Necklace, is the most famous product of the master of the ironic short story. Maupassant wrote some three hundred tales in ten years, and this set shows his range at its height.

Mathilde Loisel borrows a necklace for a ball, loses it, and spends ten years in poverty replacing it. The close, the original was paste, lands with the quiet cruelty that became Maupassant's signature in the tale. Other pieces here turn on peasants' cunning, soldiers' lust, and the small revenges of the slighted and the poor. His prose wastes no word, and each ending reframes all that came before it in the story. School readers meet him here first, and few forget the snap of his endings.
maeterlinck-plays-1902:
Maurice Maeterlinck, a Belgian writer who worked in French, wrote the plays translated here in the 1890s. The English book appeared in 1902. Alladine and Palomides is a brief tale of doomed love in a castle. Pelleas and Melisande tells of a love that leads to death in a dark kingdom.

The Death of Tintagiles shows a child prince threatened by unseen powers. Maeterlinck was a leader of Symbolist drama, which favors mood and suggestion over action. His figures speak softly and often seem to wait for fate. These plays shaped modern theatre and also inspired famous music, including an opera by Debussy.
dunbar-sport-of-gods-1902:
Paul Laurence Dunbar published The Sport of the Gods in 1902, a novel about a Black family from the South. Berry Hamilton is a loyal former servant accused of a theft he did not commit. He goes to prison, and his family moves to New York City. The city promises freedom but brings new harms.

His wife, son, and daughter each face temptation, crime, and despair. Dunbar shows how racism and city life work together to crush them. The title points to forces that treat human lives as playthings. The novel was an early and bleak portrait of the move north later called the Great Migration.
kipling-just-so-stories-1902:
Rudyard Kipling published Just So Stories in 1902, a book of tales he first told his own children. Each story explains, in playful fashion, how an animal got its trait. The whale gets its throat, the camel its hump, and the leopard its spots. The tales begin in the high and far-off times.

Kipling mixes prose with poems and speaks straight to the reader as Best Beloved. The stories draw on India, Africa, and the sea. Their rhythm begs to be read aloud. Generations of families have kept the book in print. It shows Kipling at his warmest and most inventive.
kant-prolegomena-carus-1902:
Immanuel Kant published the Prolegomena to Any Future Metaphysics in 1783, two years after his first Critique. The English text here is Paul Carus's translation of 1902. Kant wrote the book to explain his ideas more clearly after critics misread the Critique. He asks how pure mathematics and pure science are possible.

His answer is that the mind imposes forms on all experience. Space, time, and the categories structure what we can know. Kant also answers the skeptic David Hume, who had woken him from dogmatic slumber. The Prolegomena is the best gateway to transcendental idealism. It prepares readers for the harder Critique itself.
ostrogorski-democracy-parties-vol-1-1902:
M. Ostrogorski's study of party machines, Volume 1, appears in Frederick Clarke's translation of 1902. The full title covers the way parties are run, with England as this volume's case. Ostrogorski lays bare the caucus system: the machine of local bosses, whips, and wire-pullers. He shows how machines capture the free choice of voters.

The book is the first close study of party machines in the modern age. Ostrogorski feared parties would replace voters as the real actors in public life. His cure was short-lived leagues for one cause in place of fixed parties. Few took the cure, yet all cite his findings. Clarke's version made the work a classic.
engels-origin-family-1902:
In The Origin of the Family, Private Property and the State, Engels turned the notes of Marx into one sweeping story. He also drew on the field work of Lewis Henry Morgan on kinship among Native peoples. Ernest Untermann translated this English edition, published in 1902. The book is the charter text of Marxist anthropology.

Engels traces family forms from group marriage to the modern household, linking each step to changes in property and farming. He argues that the monogamous family, private wealth, and the state all rose together. Critics have faulted his sources, but the book shaped a century of debate on kinship and power.
hobson-imperialism-1902:
John Atkinson Hobson was a British journalist and economist who reported from South Africa before writing Imperialism: A Study in 1902. He asked why rich nations were racing to seize colonies across Africa and Asia. His answer pointed home, to the flow of money itself.

Hobson argues that the rich save more than they can spend at home, a fault he calls underconsumption. Surplus capital then hunts for profit abroad, and flags and armies follow the investments. Lenin read the book closely and named it as a source for his own theory of imperialism. Hobson wrote with direct sight of the South African war and its costs.
kropotkin-mutual-aid-1902:
Peter Kropotkin published Mutual Aid: A Factor of Evolution in 1902. Kropotkin, a Russian prince turned rebel and a trained geographer, had watched animal life in Siberia. He argued that working together, not just struggle, drives the change of species and helps them survive hard times.

Chapters survey help among animals, early human clans, medieval towns, and modern workers. Kropotkin answered Darwin's followers who stressed struggle alone, using field reports and past records as proof. The book became the base text for his free, shared way of life without rulers. It also shaped later study of how living things help each other thrive.
bennett-anna-five-towns-1902:
Arnold Bennett grew up in the Staffordshire Potteries, the five towns that fill much of his fiction. Anna of the Five Towns, published in 1902, was the novel that first made his name. It draws closely on the strict chapel world he knew as a young man.

Anna Tellwright inherits money of her own, yet her miserly father keeps tight control of her life. She must choose between a dutiful engagement and a love she truly feels. Bennett shows the cost of saving, duty, and gossip in a small industrial town. The novel remains a key work of English regional realism.
conrad-typhoon-1902:
Joseph Conrad drew Typhoon from his own years as a merchant navy officer in eastern seas. The novella first appeared in magazine form and was published as a book in 1902. It is one of his most direct and powerful sea stories.

Captain MacWhirr, a stolid and literal-minded man, refuses to steer around a coming storm in the China Sea. His ship, the Nan-Shan, sails straight into the typhoon with a cargo of Chinese laborers below deck. Conrad renders the storm's force in famous detail. The real subject is MacWhirr himself: dim, stubborn, and somehow exactly the man the crisis needs.
gorky-lower-depths-1902:
The Lower Depths, Maxim Gorky's play of 1902, reached English in Jenny Covan's translation of 1922. The scene is a night lodging house in a Russian city, run by a hard landlord and his wife. Thieves, ruined nobles, sick women, and a former actor fill its bunks and argue through the night.

An old pilgrim named Luka comforts each lodger with kind, useful lies. When he vanishes, hope collapses and the actor hangs himself offstage. The Moscow Art Theatre made the play a triumph under Stanislavsky in 1902. Gorky asks whether truth or mercy serves the desperate better. The question, never settled, keeps the play alive.
novalis-henry-ofterdingen-1802:
Henry of Ofterdingen, Novalis's unfinished novel, appeared in 1802, after his early death, and in English in 1842. Henry, a young poet of medieval Germany, dreams of a blue flower and sets out to seek its meaning. His road leads through merchants, miners, crusaders, and hermits, each teaching him part of poetry's secret.

Tales within the tale, songs, and visions carry Henry further than any map could. The blue flower became the central emblem of German Romantic longing. Novalis meant the novel as an answer to Goethe's Wilhelm Meister, exalting poetry over prose life. His friend Tieck published the fragment, and its spell has never lifted. Few unfinished books have shaped a movement so deeply.
novalis-disciples-at-sais-1802:
Una Birch translated The Disciples at Saïs into English in 1903, in her Methuen edition of Novalis. The fragment, left unfinished at Novalis's death in 1801, gathers young seekers at the temple of Isis in Egypt. They debate how nature hides her secrets and how the heart may learn them.

Some trust study, some trust love, and a fairy tale within the fragment gives its own answer. Birch's volume adds Novalis's famous fragments on poetry, faith, and the world. Together they state the Romantic creed in its purest form: nature and spirit are one book. The prose is dense yet luminous, meant for slow reading. It remains a source text for students of Romantic thought.
rilke-buch-der-bilder-1902:
Das Buch der Bilder, The Book of Images, is Rainer Maria Rilke's early book of poems, published in German in 1902. The text here is the German original, since no English translation is in the public domain. Rilke was still in his twenties, fresh from Russia trips and deep study of art.

The poems picture saints, angels, lovers, beggars, and quiet rooms, each held in a tender, watchful gaze. Things in Rilke are never mere props; they seem to look back at the reader. His lines favor soft music over bold statement, and images over argument. The book stands at the source of modern German lyric poetry. Later came the sterner Elegies, but the seeds are here.
arabian-nights-burton-1885-vol-02:
Burton's second volume of the Thousand Nights and a Night appeared in 1885, in step with the first. Shahrazad's nightly bargain with King Shahryar continues: each dawn leaves a tale unfinished, and her life is spared one more day. The stories in this stretch widen the book's world of caliphs, fishermen, and enchanters.

Baghdad under Harun al-Rashid begins to loom large in Burton's pages. Lovers, thieves, and wandering dervishes take their turns inside tales within tales. Burton's English mixes archaisms with street talk to match the Arabic shifts of tone. His footnotes, learned and earthy, run beside the text throughout. Readers who finish volume one meet here the cycle in full flood.
arabian-nights-burton-supplemental-1886-:
Volume two of Burton's Supplemental Nights, issued from 1886 onward, continues the further tales beyond the main ten volumes. Burton gathered them from Arabic manuscripts that the standard cycle left out. Shahrazad's frame still governs, but the store now draws on wider and later sources.

The tales here share the main set's mixture of wonder, romance, and rough comedy. Burton translates with the same literal care and loads the same learned notes. For scholars, the supplement preserves stories that tidier editions never print at all. For readers, it is simply more Nights, told in the established voice. The Gutenberg text is ebook 3446. Burton's appetite for the whole tradition drives every page.
ocean-of-story-kathasaritsagara-tawney-1:
Volume two of The Ocean of Story, in Penzer's edition of Tawney's translation from 1924, continues Somadeva's Kathasaritsagara. The frame hero, Naravahanadatta, gathers the tales that will attend his rise as king of the Vidyadharas. Each book adds fresh streams of story to the ocean Somadeva promised.

Merchants sail to golden islands, fools outwit kings, and faithful wives undo curses in these middle reaches. Penzer's footnotes trace motifs from India to Iceland, tale by tale. Tawney translated the whole vast cycle while serving in India, a feat of stamina in itself. The edition's ten volumes restore a work English readers once knew only in extracts. Volume two keeps the current strong.
thomson-bible-1808-vol-02:
The second volume of Charles Thomson's 1808 Bible carries the story from the first book of Kings through Esther. It then adds the wisdom books, from Job through the Song of Solomon. Thomson translated from the Greek Septuagint, and Jane Aitken printed the volumes at Philadelphia.

Readers meet Solomon's temple, the split of the kingdom, exile and return, and the court tale of Esther. Then the tone shifts to poetry: Job's debate, the Psalms in Greek order, Proverbs, and the Song. Because Thomson worked from Greek, names and lines often differ from the King James text. The volume shows the Bible as the Greek church read it.
paulus-aegineta-seven-books-adams-vol-02:
The second volume of Francis Adams's English Paul of Aegina appeared in 1846. Paul, a Greek physician of the seventh century, wrote the Seven Books as a complete guide to the healing art. This middle volume carries on his survey of disease and cure through the body.

The books treat fevers in their kinds, then the ills of the head, the eyes, the chest, and the gut, with the drugs and diets for each. Paul writes as a working doctor, short and sure. His handbook ruled medicine from Baghdad to Paris for a thousand years. Adams, a Scottish country doctor himself, notes where his own practice matched the ancient text.
browne-literary-history-of-persia-vol-1-:
Edward G. Browne, the Cambridge orientalist who gave his life to Persia, opened his Literary History of Persia in 1902. This first volume runs from the earliest times to Firdawsi, the poet of the Shahnameh. It is still the classic English survey of Persian letters. The title page is missing from this scan, but the text is complete from the preface.

Browne moves from the Avesta and the inscriptions of kings through the Arab conquest to the rebirth of Persian verse. Rudaki, Daqiqi, and Firdawsi close the arc, with long extracts in his own translation. He writes as a lover of the land as much as a scholar. Every later student of Persian Sufi poetry starts in Browne's garden.
eckartshausen-wolke-1802:
Karl von Eckartshausen published Die Wolke über dem Heiligthum, The Cloud upon the Sanctuary, in German in 1802. The book is built as six letters, each one addressed to a seeking reader. Its theme is the interior Church, a hidden fellowship of the elect that lives within the outer one.

Eckartshausen teaches that this inner Church keeps the deepest truths of faith alive across the ages. His letters move quietly, urging the reader inward rather than toward new rites or orders. The work carried Rosicrucian and theosophic ideas into the 1800s with real force. Later groups, from the Golden Dawn to the Martinists, drew on its vision.
scheible-das-kloster-vol02:
Band two of Das Kloster, issued by editor Johann Scheible in 1845, gathers cells five through eight. Scheible's plan was bold for its time: rescue the cheap print of past ages before it rotted away. Whole texts went back into print under his Stuttgart imprint, in German, for any buyer to own.

Folk magic fills much of the space, from charms spoken over wounds to full spell books. Faust tales and Höllenzwänge, the hell-compelling grimoires, keep their full wording here. Chapbooks of popular story stand beside them without apology. Scholars still mine these pages when a lone copy elsewhere has crumbled or vanished.
voltaire-philosophical-dictionary-1802:
Voltaire published his Dictionnaire philosophique in 1764, a pocket book of short articles meant to be carried and quoted. The London English edition of 1802, The Philosophical Dictionary, is the text here. He wrote many entries himself and shaped them all into an alphabet of the Enlightenment, from Abraham to Zoroaster.

Toleration, fanaticism, and superstition take the sharpest hits, while common sense gets the warmest praise. Each article is a small raid: a definition, a story, a sting in the tail. Voltaire meant the book to change the way his century thought, one entry at a time. It remains the most readable of his weapons, and the most quoted.
gibbs-elementary-statistical-mechanics-1:
Elementary Principles in Statistical Mechanics, from 1902, was the one book J. Willard Gibbs shaped as a whole. In it he founds statistical mechanics, the study of how vast groups of particles act. Rather than track each particle, Gibbs studies whole ensembles of possible systems. From those ensembles he derives the behavior of heat and energy.

The canonical distribution, his central tool, states how energy spreads among a system's states. Entropy gains a clear statistical meaning in his hands. The book's math is dense, yet its plan is clean. Physicists treat it as a founding text. It gave physics its statistical soul, as one summary puts it.
hilbert-foundations-geometry-townsend-19:
David Hilbert rebuilt geometry on strict axioms in The Foundations of Geometry, Englished by E. J. Townsend in 1902. The text here is the second edition of Hilbert's German work. He starts from undefined terms and a short list of axioms. Every theorem must follow from those axioms alone, with no help from pictures.

Hilbert tests his axioms for consistency and for freedom from hidden overlap. He shows which theorems fall if a given axiom is dropped. The rigor of the method set a new standard for all mathematics. Teachers call the book the axiomatic method's manifesto. Readers need patience, and gain precision. Its influence spread to every exact science.
young-journal-of-discourses-vol02:
Liverpool printed Volume II of the Journal of Discourses in 1855, one more year of Utah sermons set in type. Brigham Young speaks often, joined by his counsellors, members of the Twelve, and other elders. Shorthand reporters caught the words as spoken, so the record keeps the rough edge of live preaching.

The talks mix high doctrine with farming, building, and conduct in a desert kingdom taking shape. Together the volumes form a year-by-year account of what the Saints heard from their pulpits. For students of the movement, few sources put them so close to the voices that led it.
das-journey-to-lhasa-1902:
Sarat Chandra Das slipped into Tibet in disguise and wrote Journey to Lhasa and Central Tibet, edited by W. W. Rockhill in 1902. Das, a Bengali schoolmaster and scholar of Tibetan, made secret journeys in 1881 and 1882 for the British survey. His narrative opens a closed land: monasteries, officials, mountain roads, and the great city of Lhasa itself.

Few outsiders saw nineteenth-century Tibet from inside, and fewer still wrote of it so fully and so well. Das paid for his knowledge with suspicion, illness, and hardship on his return to India. The book remains a primary Western source on the old Tibet before modern change swept through it.
crawley-the-mystic-rose-1902:
Ernest Crawley's 1902 study of primitive marriage took on a subject few scholars had treated directly: sexual taboo. He argued that fear and prohibition, not free early love, shaped the first rules of marriage and contact between the sexes.

Crawley examines seclusion rites, the dread of contagion through touch, and the religious force behind bans on certain unions. He ranges across peoples and periods in search of the roots of these prohibitions. His claim was that taboo made individuals distinct and society possible. The book pioneered the study of taboo and influenced later writers on marriage and purity rules.
dewey-child-curriculum-1902:
The Child and the Curriculum, published in 1902, is Dewey's short classic on the central quarrel of schooling. Reformers fought over whether education should follow the child's nature or the demands of the subject matter; Dewey argues the quarrel itself is false.

The child and the curriculum, he says, are two ends of one process: the child's present experience and the organized knowledge of the race. Teaching is the art of guiding the one into the other without crushing either. The essay is barely fifty pages and has never gone out of use. It remains the clearest statement of Dewey's educational faith.
cooley-human-nature-social-order-1902:
Human Nature and the Social Order, published in 1902, is Charles Horton Cooley's founding text of what became symbolic interactionism. The American sociologist argues that self and society are twins: neither exists apart from the other.

His famous concept is the looking-glass self: we imagine how we appear to others, imagine their judgment of that appearance, and feel pride or shame accordingly. Through such mirrors, persons are made in communication. Cooley writes gently, with a novelist's eye for inner life. The book reshaped American sociology and social psychology, and its central image is still in daily use.
hastings-dictionary-bible-vol4-1902:
Volume Four of Hastings's Dictionary of the Bible, published in 1902, completes the main alphabet, from Pleroma to Zuzim. James Hastings had driven the huge project for a decade. The final alphabetical volume was long awaited by subscribers.

Long articles on prophecy, the Psalms, Rome, sacrifice, and the Temple anchor this volume. Writers sum up the scholarship of the 1890s on the Bible's history and teaching. The set's balance of faith and learning made it a fixture in seminaries. Readers today use it to see how the best scholars of 1900 understood the scriptures. Sets were sold volume by volume to ministers across the English-speaking world.
encyclopaedia-biblica-vol3-1902:
Volume Three of the Encyclopaedia Biblica, from 1902, covers L to P. Cheyne and Black's critical dictionary was now the standard proof that Bible study had changed forever. Its articles assume readers who want evidence, not comfort.

Major entries treat the Law, the Messiah, Palestine, the Pharisees, and the prophets. Natural history articles identify the plants and animals of scripture with care. The volume also maps tribal lands and traces place names through the sources. Critics attacked its doubts; students mined its facts. Either way, no serious Bible library of 1902 was complete without it. Signed initials at each article's end name the scholar who stands behind it.
plos-pone-0003402:
Karoliina Harkonmäki and co-authors asked how far genes shape early retirement in this 2008 study. They followed about 24,000 Finnish twins for thirty years. Records showed which twins left work early due to disability. Common causes included depression and other major illnesses.

Comparing twin pairs let the team split genetic effects from life experience. Genes did carry part of the risk of disability retirement. The share differed by the medical cause behind the retirement. The findings inform debates on work ability, welfare, and fair support for sick workers. Twin studies remain one of the few ways to split those two forces apart.
plos-pone-0003502:
Nicholas P. Holmes, Charles Spence, and Peter C. Hansen scanned brains during tool use in this 2008 study. Holding a tool merges touch at the hand with sights far away. The brain must link those split sources into one event. They tested attention shifts while people felt vibrations through a simple tool.

Brain imaging showed how attention networks handle that split. Tool use changed which locations drew multisensory attention. The results map part of the neural choreography of tool skill. Such skill sits near the root of human technology. Tools extend the body in the mind as well as in the hand.
plos-pone-0003602:
Kelly B. Wyatt and co-authors studied a mammal die-off on Christmas Island in this 2008 paper. Christmas Island sits in the Indian Ocean. Its native mammals vanished in a historical extinction event. Novel infectious disease can drive declines and even extinction in some animal groups.

For mammals, well-corroborated disease extinctions were still lacking. The team's evidence correlated the island losses with introduced infectious disease. Arriving pathogens, not just habitat loss, may erase a fauna. The case strengthens disease as an extinction force. Island species are most at risk, since they evolved with few germs around.
plos-pone-0003702:
Xiaosi Gu, Xun Liu, Kevin G. Guise, and colleagues published this psychology study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Alexithymia is a trait marked by trouble knowing, handling, or describing one's own feelings. Brain scans have tied it to weaker activity in a region that helps control thought. The authors tested healthy adults.

They compared people high and low in the alexithymic trait on voluntary control tasks. The study probes how a blind spot for one's own emotions relates to steering attention on purpose. It links a personality trait to the mechanics of mental control in everyday life.
plos-pone-0003802:
J. R. Managbanag, Tarynn M. Witten, Danail Bonchev, and colleagues published this aging study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Finding genes that modulate longevity is a major goal of aging research. Such genes could become targets for treatment as well as keys to basic biology. The authors took a network approach.

They applied shortest-path analysis to gene networks, tracing the shortest routes between known aging-related genes. Genes lying on those paths became candidates for affecting lifespan. The network approach offers a new compass for aging research beyond one-gene-at-a-time hunts. The method can be reused for other traits tied to long life.
plos-pone-0003902:
Bindi Thomas, John D. Holland, and Edward O. Minot tracked an elephant by satellite for five years. Their 2008 PLOS ONE article follows an African elephant cow, Loxodonta africana. Tracking ran from September 2003 to August 2008. The cow ranged across Sabi Sand Reserve and Kruger National Park.

GPS records showed her daily movements over the whole period. She was confirmed as part of a group of seven elephants. Long tracks like this reveal how elephants use land across seasons. Park managers can use such maps to plan fences, water, and safe corridors. The article came out in PLOS ONE, an open journal for science and health research.
plos-pone-0004002:
Liliana R. Vitorino, Gabriele Margos, Edward J. Feil, and co-authors mapped a Lyme disease relative's geography in 2008. Borrelia lusitaniae is a tick-borne spirochete of the Old World. It occurs mainly around the Mediterranean Basin. Lizards of the Lacertidae family serve as its reservoir hosts.

Their PLOS ONE article used multilocus sequence typing to sort strains. Fine-scale patterns emerged in where each strain type lives. Host lizards likely shape that patchy distribution. Knowing strain geography helps predict where human exposure may occur. The work appeared in PLOS ONE, with its methods and data open for all to see.
plos-pone-0004102:
Andrew Hollands, Ramy K. Aziz, Rita Kansal, and co-authors studied a natural mutation in strep bacteria in 2008. Group A streptococcus causes diseases from sore throat to severe invasion. Studies noted high SpeB output tracks with less invasive disease. What SpeB does during infection stayed unclear, though.

Their PLOS ONE article uses a clinical strain lacking SpeB expression. A natural mutation in the ropB gene suppressed SpeB in that strain. The same change reduced systemic virulence of M1T1 strep. The result helps untangle a long-standing pattern in strep epidemiology. The full report sits in PLOS ONE, free to read with all its data shown.
plos-pone-0004202:
Camille Martinand-Mari and colleagues published this developmental study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Programmed cell death is one of the clearest signs of how flexible living systems are. It usually sits upstream of major patterning events, such as the shaping of fingers in vertebrates or the facets of the fly eye.

The authors studied non-proliferative epithelia, sheets of cells that no longer divide. They asked how the sheet's topology controls who lives and who dies. Topology here means the pattern of cells and their neighbours. Their work shows that in a quiet tissue, geometry itself can be a fate decision.
plos-pone-0004302:
Shahin Zangenehpour, Asif Ghazanfar, and David Lewkowicz published this primate development study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Knowing a trait's evolutionary origin means knowing how development and ancestry interact. Human infants undergo perceptual narrowing in their first year, losing some ability to match sights and sounds across species.

The team studied infant vervet monkeys, testing heterochrony, shifts in developmental timing, and cross-species intersensory matching. Comparing monkey infants with human infants shows whether narrowing is a human quirk or a primate pattern. Such comparisons anchor big claims about human development in evidence. Monkeys and humans share much early development, so the test is a fair one.
plos-pone-0004402:
Anorexia nervosa is far more often studied in women than in men. Anu Raevuori, Hans Hoek, Ezra Susser, and co-authors measured it in Finnish men. Their 2009 PLOS ONE paper screened male twins born from 1975 to 1979. The men came from the FinnTwin16 birth cohorts. In all, 2,122 men answered a screening questionnaire on lifetime eating disorders.

Men who screened positive, plus their co-twins, got closer study. Eighteen men screened positive in the first pass. Twin data let the authors check shared genes and upbringing. The study gives rare nationwide numbers for male anorexia. It shows the illness in men is uncommon but real. Those figures help correct a strong gender gap in eating-disorder research.
plos-pone-0004502: In 2009, Mishra, Singh, and Aggrawal found sugar and hormones steering roots. Glucose and auxin signaling interacted to control Arabidopsis seedling root growth. The two signals tuned young root development. The finding maps plant plasticity nicely. The roots adapt to local conditions.
plos-pone-0004602: In 2009, Lõhmus and Björklund dosed wild birds with a hunger hormone anew. Leptin affected life history decisions in a passerine bird. The neat field experiment shifted brooding choices measurably. The finding maps life trade-offs. The test hormone is leptin.
plos-pone-0004702: In 2009, a team squeezed faint isoform signals from old gene chips anew here. Gene-specific signal profiles were pulled from the chips. The tricky splice forms were split. The neat method aids gene work today well. The mRNA processing is varied still.
bell-anatomy-brain-1802:
Charles Bell mapped the brain in The Anatomy of the Brain, from 1802, with engravings of rare beauty. The Scottish surgeon traced the nerves that carry feeling apart from those that move muscle. That split, sensory against motor, remade the study of the nervous system from the ground up.

Bell drew and engraved many plates with his own skilled hand. His findings guided surgery and physiology for the century that followed him. Clear prose makes hard anatomy open to the careful reader. The book founded modern neuroanatomy in effect, and its plates still draw praise from doctors and artists alike.
burnet-telluris-theoria-sacra-1702:
Thomas Burnet builds a sacred theory of the earth in Telluris Theoria Sacra, in Latin in this 1702 printing. The earth begins smooth as an egg, cracks at the Flood, and will end in fire. Newton admired the vast scheme, while theologians attacked its bold handling of Scripture and nature alike.

Mountains are ruins, in Burnet's striking view, the wreck of a fairer world. Poetry and geology blend in his grand, flowing Latin periods throughout. He sought to wed Moses to the new science of his age. The book founded geological theorizing in the English world, and its vision haunted writers from Milton's heirs to the Romantics.
playfair-illustrations-huttonian-1802:
John Playfair explains Hutton's theory of the earth in Illustrations of the Huttonian Theory, from 1802. Slow causes, acting over deep time, shape the globe in this account. Rain, rivers, and heat from below raise and wear the land in endless cycles, with no need of sudden universal ruin to explain the rocks.

Playfair made his friend Hutton readable where the original was dense. His clear prose taught geology to think in millions of years. Unconformities in Scottish rock faces serve as his star witnesses here. The book forms the classic statement of uniformitarian geology, the doctrine on which Lyell and Darwin would later build their own world-changing works.
jesuit-relations-thwaites-vol-02:
Acadia in 1612 to 1614 is the ground of Volume 2, printed in 1896. Thwaites placed these reports second in his vast edition of the Jesuit Relations. The French missions on the Atlantic shore were still small and weak.

English raids, bitter winters, and thin supplies test the priests at every turn. Their letters home mix faith, fear, and plain facts about the land. They note Mi'kmaq customs, trade goods, and the mood of each camp. Step by step, the volume preserves the first French foothold in North America. Few records of those years are as close or as frank.
journal-of-discourses-vol-02:
Another year of Tabernacle preaching fills Volume Two, issued in 1855. Watt's shorthand again caught Brigham Young and the apostles as they spoke. The gathering of converts from abroad stands high among the themes.

Sermons sort out the order of the priesthood for a growing church. They urge the Saints to build homes, mills, and farms in the desert. Trials of the young kingdom get frank, pastoral treatment week by week. Doctrine takes shape in public speech, not in quiet study here. The founders' urgent voices carry both law and comfort to their flock. The volume sets the tone for the twenty-five that follow it.
iraq-wmd-nie-2002:
In October 2002 the American intelligence agencies issued a National Intelligence Estimate on Iraq's weapons programs. Congress had demanded the summary judgment before voting on whether to allow war against Saddam Hussein. The declassified excerpts released to the public stated the agencies' key claims in strong terms.

The estimate said with high confidence that Iraq held chemical and biological weapons and was rebuilding its nuclear program. After the 2003 invasion, search teams found no such stockpiles and no active nuclear effort. Reviews later found that weak evidence had been stated as near certainty and that doubts inside the agencies were buried. The episode became a standard case of intelligence failure, since the estimate had served as the public basis for war.
sombart-moderne-kapitalismus-vol1-1902:
Werner Sombart published the first volume of Modern Capitalism in German in 1902. Sombart, a German economist of the historical school, set out to explain how the modern economic system was born. The scale of the attempt, a full history of capitalism from its roots, matched the ambitions of its age.

Volume 1 traces the system's growth from medieval trade through the early crafts and the first great merchants. Sombart sorts economic life into stages and asks what spirit drives each one, the quiet craftsman against the bold entrepreneur. His answer gave later writers the phrase capitalist spirit to argue with. Weber, his younger rival, answered Sombart in famous essays of his own. The volume opens the most ambitious economic history of its time, and the argument it started has never fully closed.
sombart-moderne-kapitalismus-vol2-1902:
The second volume of Sombart's Modern Capitalism followed the first in 1902, completing the original design. Sombart had traced capitalism's birth in the opening volume; now the system stands full-grown. The German scholar's panorama widens to the whole industrial order of his day.

Volume 2 carries the tale into the industrial age: the factory system, the great firms and trusts, and the world market that bound them together. Sombart weighs the costs of the triumph, the uprooted crafts and crowded cities, beside the gains in wealth and power. His historical method piles up evidence where pure theory would argue. Economic history on the grandest scale ever attempted closes here, with capitalism triumphant and troubled at once. Later editions tripled the work, but the 1902 pair remains the statement that made his name.
cia-0000008702:
June 1973 brought a summary of photo comparison analysis results, looking back across many cases at once. The CIA's specialists had spent years matching prisoner photographs against missing-person files. A summary could judge the method itself: how often it matched, and how well.

Reviews of this kind mattered because the program guided real decisions about real men. If photo matching proved weak, other leads needed more weight. The report dates from just after the Paris accords, when homecoming sharpened every open case. It shows the identification effort pausing to grade its own tools at a critical moment.
cia-0000009702:
More information on a preliminary debriefing site for captured American pilots arrived in a July 1971 CIA paper. The heading calls the paper additional, meaning earlier reports on the site already existed. Newly captured pilots passed through first questioning before reaching main prisons.

Knowing where that first stage happened helped trace a prisoner's path from capture onward. A man's route through early sites could explain later sightings or their absence. Analysts collected such details piece by piece, often from former prisoners or local sources. This file adds one layer to the map of how captivity began.
cia-0000009802:
Four American prisoners were moved to a new location in Chau Doc province, a February 1972 report states. It follows a January item placing four prisoners in the same Delta province. Read together, the two files trace one group's forced journey.

Movement reports frustrated every plan built on fixed camp locations. A rescue map aged in weeks when prisoners were marched elsewhere. For the accounting, though, movement still proved the men alive on a date. Analysts chained such reports together to keep a group's trail unbroken. This file is one link in that chain, laid down a month after the last.
cia-0000011502:
France's war in Indochina was turning against it when the CIA reviewed the situation there in January 1951. The paper pairs its survey with a map supplement on likely developments. The Viet Minh, backed by the new communist government in China, were gaining ground against French forces across Vietnam, Laos, and Cambodia.

Analysts charted the Viet Minh's gains and the strain the war placed on Paris. They also weighed how the fighting might spread or end. Coming three years before the French defeat at Dien Bien Phu, the study shows the long war's middle passage as Washington watched and worried.
cia-0000012302:
Nuclear matters lead the quoted title of a Helms memo from November 1961, sent to the DIA director. The subject line breaks off at the word Nuclear, the rest cut away in the file. The piece belongs to the Military Thought traffic: Soviet professional writing on the weapons that defined the age. Nothing the colonel's channel carried mattered more than how Moscow's officers thought about nuclear war.

The memo flowed toward year's end without the season slowing it. Value explains the pace: the intelligence was too prized to pause. For readers, the page shows the case's paperwork at its most consequential, where journal articles fed the gravest planning on earth.
cia-0000012402:
Fourteen meetings by May 4, 1961: the record of session fourteen marks a fortnight of near-continuous contact. The handlers' stamina matched the spy's, sitting after sitting. Day after day of questions could exhaust any source. Such a pace could also expose a pattern to watchers. Yet the run held, because the colonel's cover trip kept him in London and his handlers used every day of it.

The record shows the marathon ongoing, session by numbered session. Routine, in the spy world, is what success looks like from inside. For readers, the page conveys the operation's true scale.
cia-0000013302:
Where American prisoners were held in Laos is the subject of a CIA item from July 1962. The item belongs to the captivity's very first years in that kingdom. American airmen and advisers were already being taken in the kingdom's civil war by then. The 1962 pins were the first marks on a long map. That map would grow for a decade, camp by camp and name by name, across some of Asia's hardest country.

The item gives the early Laotian captivity its geography. Later files would add hundreds of reports to this beginning layer. For readers, the page is the pioneering layer of the accounting: the first locations, fixed while the secret war was young.
cia-0000013902: An American pilot prisoner lay in Military Hospital 103 at Ha Dong, in a CIA note dated November 5, 1967. A hurt airman in a northern hospital was news worth filing at once. His care, or lack of it, bore on wider claims about prisoner treatment. The note fixes one wounded man at one known place and date.
cia-0000014802: Dossier material on Anatoli Antonovich Yakovlev fills a CIA file dated January 2, 1963. The file mentions Harry Gold, Klaus Fuchs, and David Greenglass. Those three names formed the chain that broke the atomic spy ring. A dossier still updated in 1963 kept the handler's file alive long after his flight from New York.
cia-0000015402: Chicago officers closed out their dealings with Dr. Leon Davidson in a short CIA note dated January 4, 1958. By phone they told him they could not solve his problem about a space message and its sender. The records, they said, had been destroyed by the agency that judged them. Davidson replied that he had heard that before, and mentioned a new article then under Pentagon review.
cia-0000022302: Rudolf Abel asked James Donovan to call his wife and advise her, a CIA record dated in 1961 reports. Abel was the Soviet spy held in America, and Donovan was his lawyer. The request came while talk of a spy swap was in the air. A small human errand sits inside a hard Cold War bargain in this short entry.
cia-0000036302:
A CIA weekly summary for the Western Hemisphere, dated January 5, 1971, leads with Brazil. Its Brazil item covers talks aimed at winning the release of a kidnapped diplomat. Diplomat kidnappings were then a feared tactic of armed groups across Latin America.

The summary gathers the week's main events into one short briefing for busy officials. The Brazil talks sit beside other regional items, weighed and ranked for the reader. Weekly digests like this show what Washington watched most closely, week by week, across the hemisphere. Kidnapped envoys were often freed only after long talks and hard bargaining over prisoners.
cia-0000042802:
General Ponce admitted that soldiers were held on the Jesuit killings, in a CIA record dated January 1, 1990. Ponce led El Salvador's armed forces as their joint chiefs chairman. An admission from the army's own chief carried unusual weight.

Inside, the admission is recorded in the general's own terms. The army had long been accused of shielding its men from justice.
